tier_reason: case_studies/base64/REPORT.md (and SUMMARY.md, redis/REPORT.md, lz4/REPORT.md) give first-party timings against the GCC -O3 -march=native scalar C reference, but the case-study harness.c, C references, .S kernels and build_and_test.sh are not in the repo (raw 404, initial commit was 'optimize.py + 3 case study reports'), and CPU model, GCC version and repeat/warmup method are unstated. First-party numbers without reproducible code or hardware: C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Base64 decode 4.80x (64 B, 50M iters: 1.81 s vs 0.38 s, 1,767 to 8,479 MB/s), 6.23x (1 KiB, 5M iters: 1,825 to 11,365 MB/s), 6.26x (16 KiB, 200K iters: 1,857 to 11,635 MB/s) over the GCC -O3 scalar LUT decoder; LZ4 fast-path decode three runs 1.07x, 0.98x, 1.02x (author: within noise); Redis SipHash 1-2 0.96x (8 B keys), 0.97x (32 B), 0.99x tie (128 B), i.e. GCC 3-4% faster on short keys.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Reference kernels: gcc -O3 -march=native (stated in case_studies/SUMMARY.md methodology, the blog post and optimize.py); AI .S assembled with gcc; generic harness built with gcc -O2. GCC version not stated.
corrections.workload: Differential-fuzzed x86-64 assembly replacements, written by an AI model with optimize.py as scaffolding, for three extracted kernels: base64 decode (valid-input-only, no padding, length multiple of 4) timed at 64 B, 1 KiB and 16 KiB inputs; LZ4 1.10.0 fast-path decode loop on 4096-byte blocks (10M iterations); Redis 7.x SipHash 1-2 on 8-, 32- and 128-byte keys. Each benchmark is one back-to-back run (GCC then AI) of the same input with CLOCK_MONOTONIC.
corrections.caveats: All numbers are self-reported in case_studies/*/REPORT.md, case_studies/SUMMARY.md and blog/ai-assembly-vs-gcc-o3.md. The reports list the C reference, the .S assembly, harness.c and build_and_test.sh, and the blog says each case study is 'a single ./build_and_test.sh away from reproducing', but none of those files are in the repo (raw.githubusercontent.com returns 404 for case_studies/base64/b64_decode_kern.c, harness.c, build_and_test.sh, lz4/harness.c, redis/harness.c; the initial commit was 'optimize.py + 3 case study reports'), so nothing can be rerun and the faster assembly itself cannot be copied: only the optimize.py driver (scanner, prompt generator, fuzz/bench harness generator) is published. CPU model and GCC version are not stated; optimize.py's generated benchmark is a single back-to-back run on one fixed input with no warmup or repeats. The baseline is a naive scalar 256-byte-LUT decoder of unstated origin; the AI kernel is the known SSSE3 pshufb nibble-lookup technique (Mula/Lemire style) without input validation (it assumes valid base64 and no padding), and existing SIMD base64 libraries (aklomp/base64, fastbase64, simdutf) were not compared. The LZ4 timings (0.024-0.027 s for 10M iterations, about 2.5 ns per call, derived from page data) are impossible for decoding a 4096-byte block, so the LZ4 row did not measure the stated workload and is not valid evidence; it is a tie anyway (runs 1.07x, 0.98x, 1.02x). SipHash is slower than GCC. The README's 'provably outperforms GCC -O3' is overstated: verification is 100K differential-fuzz iterations per kernel, and two of three kernels are a loss or a tie. MIT is stated only in the README; there is no LICENSE file or copyright notice and GitHub shows no license. No independent coverage found; the Hacker News thread could not be opened (egress blocked).

notes: Real but weak entry: base64 decode 4.8-6.3x over a naive scalar LUT decoder is internally consistent (MB/s match iterations x size / time, derived from page data), but the asm, harness and build script are not published, so the speedup is uncheckable and nothing fast is copyable; keep at C with the shortcomings above. LZ4 numbers are implausible (about 2.5 ns per 4 KiB block decode) and SipHash is a GCC win; MIT is README-only. Last commit 2026-05-17 (FUNDING.yml), 2 stars, 0 forks, 3 commits, not a fork.
